newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr reels as Howard feeds rate paranoia.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr reels as Howard feeds rate paranoia.

text.p: The Australian dollar was sent reeling Tuesday as a single sentence from Prime Minister John Howard fed market paranoia about interest rates.
A laborious rally was brought to a bloody halt for bulls when Howard said rates had come down because of falling budget deficits and he would like to see them lower still.

The market suspected political pressure on the Reserve Bank to cut rates, an event it has lived in fear of since the last easing in May, and slashed A$ positions. Support, already sapped by broad-based weakness in commodity prices overnight, caved-in quickly and the currency crumpled to new 18-month lows.

By 4.45 pm (0645 GMT) a dazed dollar lay at US$0.7418/23, its lowest close since January 1996, from US$0.7445/50 just before Howard's one-liner was reported. It ended Monday under pressure at US$0.7440/45 having slid from US$0.7520 Friday.

Howard, speaking to a Liberal Party gathering, said; "One of the reasons why interest rates have come down in Australia, and I'd like to see them still lower ... is that we are no longer running such large deficits."
Traders were unsure if he was referring to commercial bank rates, money market rates or official rates -- or maybe all three -- but decided it was safer to assume the worst.
The market has a high regard for the RBA's independence and few seriously think the bank would ease if it did not believe the move justified on economic grounds.

However, doubts did creep in during the run-up to the last cut when government officials talked of little else but lower rates. In a speech on May 22, Treasury's representative on the RBA board, Ted Evans, argued wages growth was overstated and the economy could be run a lot faster with little risk to inflation.
When the cut came a day later the market was both surprised and suspicious, and is now hyper-sensitive to any government utterance on the topic.

Analysts have long rated the chance of a cut at about 50/50 regardless of government jawboning and reckon unemployment data Thursday and key inflation and wages figures on July 23/24 will have far more relevance.
Whatever Howard's intention, the timing could not have been worse for dollar bulls who were already under seige from falling commodity prices.

The influential Commodity Research Bureau index plunged 3.35 points Monday to a two-year low of 232.22 with the selloff led by precious metals but joined by wheat, base metals and oil. The slide brought the losses since mid-May to more than 8.0 percent.
The fall also took the index, which is closely followed by U.S. investors, well under major chart support at 236.00 and out of a rising channel which has lasted since early 1993.

The index was now within spitting distance of a 50 percent retracement of the entire rally from 198.00 in 1993 to a 257.00 peak in April last year. The next target would be a 61.8 percent retracement which would take it back to 223.00.

This was crucial for the dollar outlook since commodities make up over 60 percent of Australia's exports and offshore investors view it as an indirect way of tapping trends, which is why it has a strong historical correlation with their prices.
Most analysts had thought strengthening world growth would lead to rising commodity prices later in the year which in turn would compensate for the dollar's dwindling yield attraction.
The growth was indeed coming but commodity prices were not responding as planned, leading some to tip a retreat to 73 cents in the medium term and perhaps as far as US$0.7070 by year end.

On the crosses, the dollar edged up to 83.80/90 yen from Monday's late 83.66/76, which had been its lowest local close since August last year. In trade weighted terms it slipped to 56.5 from a previous close of 56.7.
